episode_thesis: After the 30 January 2026 silver crash, Rob Carver argues that continuous volatility-adjusted position sizing plus diversification is what protects a trend follower in parabolic reversals (his loss was 3%, while unscaled leveraged CTAs swung by tens of points), that liquidity is not constant, and that crowded volatility-adjusters can amplify sell-offs. The Man AHL paper he summarises says an investor who wants trend as equity-crisis protection and a cash source should favour traditional liquid futures, while a pure Sharpe maximiser should trade more alternative markets. Niels adds the Hunt brothers 1979 leverage lesson and the view that positioning, not the Fed-chair nomination, drove the silver sell-off.

speakers.name: Rob Carver
speakers.role: systematic futures trader and author, ex-AHL and AQR, trades a small dynamically optimised futures account
speakers.speaker_note: Main speaker. Captions are clean in most places. The remark that a 3% one-day loss was in line with other CTAs at similar volatility is Niels's (ledger correction on C05-5), not Rob's.

worldview_premises.premise: A CTA's position is a function of trend strength (forecast) and instrument volatility, so rising volatility can cut exposure even while the trend signal strengthens. Systems differ: binary long/short, continuous forecast scaling, or volatility sizing only at entry.

A normal-speed trend signal stays long after even a record one-day drop. A daily-rebalanced system sizes from the prior close and cannot cut intraday, so protection comes from having already scaled down.
Risk management comes down to position sizing and diversification. Together they limited his loss to 3% on the crash day, while concentrated or unscaled, leveraged funds lose far more.
worldview_premises.support: his own 3% loss versus reported swings of a levered CTA (+72% to +27% on the month)

worldview_premises.premise: Liquidity is not a constant. After a run-up and pullback the buyers are gone, so liquidity vanishes in crises (more in less-liquid markets), and recent volume and open interest spikes from 'tourists' overstate it; look back one to two years.
worldview_premises.support: market-structure argument (cinema with one fire door)

worldview_premises.premise: CTAs, risk parity and other quant strategies all cut exposure when volatility spikes, so crowding magnifies volatility-driven sell-offs.
A stop widened with volatility needs a smaller position at the same time, or risk rises. A stop that does not widen shakes you out of trends early, and no reasonable stop avoids a 25% one-day gap.
worldview_premises.support: design reasoning; he does not use stops

worldview_premises.premise: With volatility-targeted instruments portfolio risk depends only on correlations, so diversification forces positions to be scaled up (about 4-5x; a 15% target would otherwise give about 3%).

Volatility is more predictable than correlation (month-on-month R-squared about 0.35 versus 0.2-0.25), and means are noise. Estimate volatility (about 1 month) and correlation (about 6 months) separately, then combine.
worldview_premises.support: his own regressions, 'off the top of my head', plus academic research

worldview_premises.premise: A large part of trend returns is a risk-on/risk-off factor (about 55% for traditional markets), while alternative and esoteric markets are about one third factor and two thirds idiosyncratic, which makes them diversifying.
Futures are cash efficient (about 20-30% of cash as margin) and this matters most when cash is needed, as in 2008 when investors drew on CTAs.
worldview_premises.support: his own account (30% margin use) and the paper; 2008 history

worldview_premises.premise: Discretionary override of his system cost him: selling equities in the April 2025 tariff tantrum lost relative performance, and the systematic version did better.
Markets have largely shrugged off the president's policy shocks since early 2025, partly through a 'TACO' pattern (he backs down), so his initial expectation of a bad market was wrong.

Systematic finance has always used supervised machine learning (regression, optimisation). AI works best in tightly defined areas such as execution research with rich tick data, and much fund AI is marketing or blue-sky research.
worldview_premises.support: opinion; he describes himself as an AI skeptic

mechanism_chains.topic: Silver parabolic run and crash for a continuously vol-scaled trend follower

steps.from: silver trend strengthens (bought 27 Nov and 3 Dec at $53 and $59)
steps.to: position grows with forecast
steps.why: position is trend strength times inverse volatility

steps.from: volatility rises (sold at $71 on 31 Dec and $81 on Monday after the crash)
steps.to: position shrinks even though trend is still long
steps.why: volatility scaling

steps.from: 30 January drop (biggest one-day fall in about 45-47 years) hits a smaller position
steps.to: loss limited to 3% of account and the silver trades still profitable
steps.why: daily rebalance cannot trade the gap, but exposure was already cut and the portfolio diversified

mechanism_chains.evidence: His own trade records and prices ($53/$59 in, $71/$81 out; peak $110-120).
mechanism_chains.fails_when: The profit is measured against entry prices, so it misses the peak; he is uncertain whether he would have been better without vol-scaling at the top. His dynamic optimisation means a strong forecast does not always give a position.

mechanism_chains.topic: Unscaled leveraged CTAs in a parabolic reversal

steps.from: no continuous volatility adjustment, high leverage
steps.to: silver becomes a growing share of the portfolio during the run-up
steps.why: position value rises with price and is never cut

steps.from: one-day crash
steps.to: very large loss (a levered CTA went from roughly +50% to +25% by Rob's estimate, +72% to +27% per Niels)
steps.why: concentrated unscaled exposure

mechanism_chains.evidence: January monthly returns for unnamed CTAs; numbers differ slightly between speakers.

mechanism_chains.topic: Liquidity illusion and crowded volatility selling

steps.from: hot market with surging volume and open interest, new 'tourist' participants
steps.to: trader believes a large position can be built and exited
steps.why: treats liquidity as constant

steps.from: price moves against the position
steps.to: everyone exits at once and the liquidity is not there
steps.why: buyers are already in; liquidity disappears in crises, more in less-liquid markets

steps.from: CTAs, risk parity and quants all cut on volatility spikes
steps.to: sell-off magnified
steps.why: crowding of the same volatility rule

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Niels notes larger CTAs were selling silver through December and January, so they were a buffer during the run-up rather than a cause.

mechanism_chains.topic: Fed chair nomination as cause of the silver crash

steps.from: nominee seen as relatively sane, possibly hawkish on rates, less mainstream on QE and balance sheet
steps.to: relief reaction in markets
steps.why: market expected someone aligned with the president

steps.from: bond market reaction muted (no 50bp two-year move recalled)
steps.to: nomination probably not the true cause of the silver sell-off
steps.why: bonds are the most direct measure of the news

steps.from: chair appointed by a president demanding loyalty
steps.to: independence is unknowable; Powell was also appointed by Trump and resisted, and chairs cannot be removed and care about legacy
steps.why: precedent

mechanism_chains.evidence: Recollection of bond moves ('haven't got the figures to hand'), precedent of Powell.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: He admits no one knows what happens when Powell's term ends in May.

steps.from: every instrument targeted to the same volatility
steps.to: book risk depends only on correlations
steps.why: volatility is equalised by construction

steps.from: low correlation between instruments
steps.to: book undershoots risk target unless positions are multiplied by about 4-5
steps.why: diversification lowers book volatility

steps.from: need to estimate the book correlation
steps.to: use P&L streams over a rolling window of about 6 months (optionally exponentially weighted), which captures asset and signal correlation
steps.why: slow estimate adds negligible extra trading compared with signal-driven trading

mechanism_chains.evidence: His own calculation of the multiplier; academic estimation research.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: The fixed 0.7 correlation from his book is a ratio of trend correlation to underlying correlation, not a book correlation, so misuse biases risk.

mechanism_chains.topic: Market universe for a trend portfolio (Man AHL paper)

steps.from: traditional markets mostly factor-driven; alternative and esoteric mostly idiosyncratic
steps.to: an unconstrained Sharpe-maximising portfolio is about 30% traditional and 70% alternative (about 5% crypto)
steps.why: idiosyncratic returns diversify

steps.from: optimising only over periods when equities fell
steps.to: about 50% traditional markets
steps.why: crisis payoff comes from the factor: short equities, long bonds; alternatives trade like risk-on assets and may be hard to short or illiquid

steps.from: adding a cash-efficiency constraint
steps.to: about 70% traditional and 30% alternative
steps.why: alternative markets need more margin, some 100%; cash efficiency matters most when cash is needed (2008)

mechanism_chains.evidence: Paper's optimisations (figures read out by Rob).
mechanism_chains.fails_when: The 30/70 optimum is unconstrained, and large CTAs cannot do it because of capacity.

steps.from: many markets trending strongly (high trend barometer)
steps.to: forecast-scaled system carries more risk
steps.why: positions scale with forecast strength

mechanism_chains.evidence: His own account: risk 'a little bit higher than it has been for a while', which matches the barometer.

decision_process.practice: Continuously adjust each position for changes in volatility as well as forecast strength (daily rebalance from the prior close).
Trade a dynamically optimised subset of 250 futures matching an idealised large portfolio; skip instruments barred by regulation or too illiquid or expensive.
decision_process.why: small account, so may hold no position despite a strong forecast

decision_process.practice: Do not use stop-losses. If using a volatility-based stop, widen it only together with a smaller position.
decision_process.why: stops do not remove gap risk; position size determines the loss

decision_process.practice: Judge liquidity over a one to two year history, not recent volume or open interest.
decision_process.why: tourists inflate volume in hot markets

decision_process.practice: Scale all positions up by about 4-5x so the diversified book hits its risk target.

Estimate book correlation from combined P&L (rolling six months, optionally exponentially weighted) and estimate volatility separately (about one month). With vol-targeted instruments, portfolio construction only needs correlations.
decision_process.why: different predictability and speed of change

decision_process.practice: Scale positions with forecast strength in each market and accept that realised risk rises when many markets trend at once.
Stay systematic and avoid discretionary overrides.
decision_process.why: his April 2025 equity sale cost relative performance

speakers.evidence_style: Own trade records and calculations (silver prices, 3% loss, 4-5x multiplier, R-squared figures from memory), reading of papers (Man AHL, FT Alphaville article), history (2008, Hunt via Niels), and first-principles reasoning on liquidity and crowding. He admits forecast errors openly.

current_views.view: Silver crash lesson is risk management (position sizing and diversification). His own loss was 3%, and his trend signal in silver remained long but the position was sold on Monday as volatility rose.
current_views.reasoning: vol-scaling cut exposure into the crash

current_views.view: The Fed-chair nomination was probably not the real cause of the silver sell-off, and the new chair's independence is unknowable.
current_views.reasoning: muted two-year yield reaction; Powell precedent

current_views.view: His trend portfolio is coping with dislocations in quant equity factors, Bitcoin and AI stocks. Most CTAs trading Bitcoin were probably short after the sell-off, and it was his biggest short position.
January trend profits came from idiosyncratic sources (gold, silver, natural gas), not from the risk-on/risk-off factor (bonds flat, equities slightly up).
Markets have shrugged off the president's policies; his own bearish call a year earlier was wrong.
current_views.reasoning: TACO pattern or nobody takes threats seriously

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: host, Top Traders Unplugged, veteran hedge fund manager; builds the Trend barometer
speakers.speaker_note: Host who states views on silver history, crowding, manager selection and AI. Listener questions he reads (Pedro) are not his views. The 3% crash-day loss being decent is his comment (ledger correction on C05-5).

worldview_premises.premise: Larger CTAs reduce silver notional as volatility expands, so they dampen rather than cause parabolic moves.
worldview_premises.support: recollection of how large CTAs behaved through December and January; cocoa episode as precedent

worldview_premises.premise: Leverage with borrowed money, pyramiding and exchange margin hikes force liquidation in parabolic moves; the same pattern recurs across eras (Hunt 1979, January 2026).
Experienced managers avoid emotional attachment and manage risk systematically.
Silver is not gold: only about 30% is mined as silver, so supply is less controllable and the market more volatile. Traders became complacent after the precious-metals rally.
Commodities belong in a trend universe because they offer opportunities, often independent of equity risk-off events (natural gas up 60% then down 26% in a day).
worldview_premises.support: the natural gas example and years of advocacy on the show

worldview_premises.premise: The silver sell-off was driven by crowded positioning (including Chinese retail), not by the Fed chair news.
Being a systematic diversified investor beats trying to interpret political and market events discretionarily.
worldview_premises.support: none beyond Rob's own discretionary example

worldview_premises.premise: A trend barometer reading shows how many tracked markets trend (64 = 64%), which indicates breadth supportive for CTAs.
Differences between trend managers come mainly from the markets they trade, not better models or faster signals.
Manager choice depends on investor objective: maximise standalone Sharpe by trading more markets, but pick traditional liquid futures managers for equity-crisis protection and cash needs.
Alphabet doubling AI capex to $185 billion suggests a possible bubble, and however high markets go it could still end badly because of building risks (timing unknowable).

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Speaker correction applied: the 3% crash-day loss being 'in line with other CTAs at similar annual volatility' is Niels's comment, not Rob's.
Numbers for the unscaled CTA's January swing differ between speakers (Rob: about 50% to 25% up; Niels: 72% to 27%). Both are unnamed and unverified.

Rob says the Fed-chair news was 'supposedly' the proximate cause yet gives only a recollection of the two-year yield move ('haven't got the figures to hand'); Niels has rumours of an investment-bank cause that he declines to repeat.

Tension between claims on crowding: Rob says vol-adjusters amplify sell-offs, Niels says large CTAs sold through the run-up and dampen. Both can hold (rise versus crash phase) but neither gives data on position sizes in silver.
Rob's profit claim on the silver trades compares entry and exit prices only and ignores the move to $110-120 in between and the effect of his dynamic optimisation.
Man AHL percentages (55/45, 1/3-2/3, 30/70, 50, 70/30, 5% crypto) are relayed from a paper that neither speaker has in front of them; Rob says 'about half' then 'more like 45-55'.
Rob's regression figures (R-squared 0.35 for volatility, 0.2-0.25 for correlation) are given 'off the top of my head'. His guess that Pedro's 0.7 comes from his book is also flagged as a gut feeling.
The silver supply fact (30% mined as silver) is second-hand ('I've heard stories').

Rob says he is wary of the FT article's AI claims because the authors are talking their own book, yet accepts its convergence thesis in workflow and pay as interesting; he supplies no evidence on how much AI funds really use.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Trend barometer and breadth (share of markets trending), which Rob links to his realised risk; margin requirements and exchange margin changes in parabolic markets; liquidity measured over one to two years; correlation between instrument P&L streams (about 6 months) and volatility (about 1 month) as risk inputs; two-year yield reaction as the cleanest read of Fed news; the Fed-chair path from May and the Supreme Court ruling on governor removal. Horizon: days to months for positions, with trend lookbacks implied but not stated.
reader_inferences: (reader) Rob's protection claim depends on volatility rising before the break; a gap that arrives with no preceding volatility rise would hit a vol-scaled book as hard as an unscaled one.

(reader) The crisis-alpha recommendation (about 50% traditional in equity-down periods) implies that a diversified CTA with many alternatives has less equity-crisis payoff than headline Sharpe suggests.
(reader) Both speakers treat positioning and leverage, not macro news, as the proximate cause of the metals crash, which implies margin and open-interest data as the observable lead input.
